questions.q: Why would benchmarking Shor's algorithm against trial division instead of the General Number Field Sieve be dishonest?
options: The General Number Field Sieve is a quantum algorithm, so it can't be used as a classical baseline
Trial division is not the best known classical factoring algorithm, so the comparison overstates the real gap against the actual competing approach
Trial division is actually faster than Shor's algorithm in all cases
Trial division and Shor's algorithm solve different problems entirely
questions.explain: Rule 1 of honest benchmarking is comparing against the best known classical algorithm. The General Number Field Sieve, not trial division, is the real classical competitor, and using a weak baseline inflates the apparent advantage.

questions.q: Why does Grover's O(√N) result need to specify what is being counted?
options: Because oracle queries, total gate count, and wall-clock time can give three different numbers, and conflating them is a common source of overstated claims
Because √N is not a well-defined mathematical quantity
Because O(√N) is only a theoretical result with no connection to any real circuit
Because Grover's algorithm has no oracle in its actual implementation
questions.explain: O(√N) refers specifically to the number of oracle queries. The oracle itself may require many gates to implement, so query count, gate count, and wall-clock time are distinct metrics that don't automatically agree.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the real blocker preventing Shor's algorithm from breaking RSA-2048 today?
options: The algorithm has never been mathematically proven correct
Shor's algorithm only works on numbers smaller than 100
RSA-2048 cannot be represented as a quantum circuit
Qubit count and hardware error rates, not a flaw in the algorithm itself, which is polynomial-time and mathematically sound
questions.explain: Chapter 5 established that the algorithm is sound; the gap is purely in hardware — current devices have far fewer qubits and far higher error rates than the millions of high-quality qubits estimates like Gidney & Ekerå (2019) suggest would be needed.

questions.q: Why is 'O(√N) beats O(N)' not automatically a guarantee that quantum hardware wins today at a given search problem?
options: Classical computers cannot perform search at all

Asymptotic growth-rate comparisons only guarantee a win for sufficiently large N; at smaller or practically relevant sizes, constant-factor overhead and hardware limitations can still favor the classical approach
Quantum hardware does not exist in any form today
O(√N) is actually a slower growth rate than O(N) for all N
questions.explain: Asymptotic notation describes behavior as N grows large; it says nothing about which approach wins at the particular N and hardware constants relevant in practice today.

questions.q: Why do Deutsch-Jozsa and Simon's algorithm require stating their 'promise' explicitly in any honest benchmark?
options: Because their entire speedup depends on the input satisfying a specific guaranteed structure (constant-or-balanced, or exactly 2-to-1 with a hidden mask) that real-world data is not guaranteed to have
Because the promise is only relevant to Grover's algorithm, not these two
Because these algorithms don't actually use oracles
Because the promise makes the problems classically unsolvable
questions.explain: Both algorithms are promise problems: the stated speedup is conditional on the function having the assumed structure. Omitting that condition misrepresents how often the speedup actually applies to real data.
